summary: Defines behavioral characteristics of Internet firewalls and requirements for their interoperability. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A firewall is a gatekeeper for a network. This describes how gatekeepers should behave so they work well with others.

questions: how should an internet firewall behave
what is a firewall transparency rule
subtitle: Defining how firewalls should behave transparently on networks.

tldr.problem: Firewall behavior was underspecified or inconsistent, causing legitimate applications to fail mysteriously when passing through firewalls because firewalls blocked necessary protocol features.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2979 establishes a transparency rule: firewalls must not cause unintended failures of standards-compliant usage that would work without the firewall present. It specifies what applications can expect and what firewalls must allow for common protocols like ICMP, SMTP, and others.
tldr.outcome: The RFC improves firewall deployments by requiring them to be transparent to legitimate traffic while still allowing sites to block illegitimate access as they see fit.

today: RFC 2979 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted and continues to define expectations for firewall behavior.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A firewall is an agent that screens network traffic, blocking or modifying traffic it deems inappropriate, dangerous, or both. Firewalls differ from Network Address Translation (NAT) functions, though the same device may provide both.

Internet usage has grown to include mission-critical applications. Many organizations want direct communications between the sometimes-hostile public Internet and their internal networks that handle valuable data or vital services. Firewalls protect these internal networks by standing on the path between the Internet and the inside, making security decisions about each packet or protocol exchange.

The problem RFC 2979 addresses is that firewall behavior is often unspecified or underspecified, leading to practical problems: legitimate applications fail in ways that are hard to diagnose because the firewall blocks something essential to the protocol without the application or administrator realizing why.
sections.eli5: Networks now need to let outside traffic in and out, but safely. Firewalls do that, but if they are poorly designed, good applications mysteriously stop working.

sections.title: How Firewalls Work
sections.content:
Firewalls work in two main ways: as protocol endpoints or as packet filters, or as some combination.

When acting as a protocol endpoint (like a SMTP client/server or HTTP proxy), a firewall can implement a safe subset of the protocol, perform extensive validity checks, use careful implementation methodologies, or run in an insulated environment. The firewall itself is visible as a protocol participant that the application communicates with directly.

When acting as a packet filter, the firewall examines each packet and then passes it through unchanged, drops it entirely, or handles it itself. The firewall is transparent to the protocol; applications do not know it is there.

Firewalls typically base decisions on IP source and destination addresses and port numbers. Common examples include blocking packets claiming to originate from the internal network but arriving from the Internet, blocking remote TELNET or RLOGIN connections, requiring SMTP and FTP to go through authorized systems, acting as an intermediate server for SMTP and HTTP, or requiring the SOCKS access protocol to tunnel through the firewall.
sections.eli5: Firewalls either sit in the middle pretending to be a server, or just look at packets and decide yes/no on each one.

sections.title: The Transparency Rule
sections.content:
The core requirement of RFC 2979 is the transparency rule:

The introduction of a firewall and any associated tunneling or access negotiation facilities MUST NOT cause unintended failures of legitimate and standards-compliant usage that would work were the firewall not present.

When failures do occur, the responsibility lies with the firewall and associated software, not with implementations of the protocols themselves. Changes to existing protocol implementations or the protocols themselves MUST NOT be necessary to work with a firewall.

This does not mean a firewall must allow everything. A site is entitled to block any access it deems illegitimate, regardless of whether the blocked traffic is standards-compliant. The transparency requirement only applies to legitimate protocol usage and unintended failures.

Firewalls MAY provide additional facilities for authentication and authorization (such as SOCKS), and may be configurable to require them. However, they MUST also allow configurations where such facilities are not required for traversal.
sections.eli5: The rule: if it is normal traffic that would work without a firewall, the firewall must let it through. Block the bad stuff, but do not break good applications.

sections.title: Examples of the Transparency Rule
sections.content:
Path MTU Discovery and ICMP: ICMP messages are often blocked because they are perceived as security risks. But this breaks Path MTU Discovery. If a firewall permits outgoing packets with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set, it MUST NOT block incoming ICMP Destination Unreachable/Fragmentation Needed errors in response. Otherwise, standard-compliant applications get mysteriously slow or broken connections.

SMTP Extensions: The original SMTP protocol did not provide extension negotiation. When RFC 1869 added EHLO, some firewalls simply added EHLO to the list of allowed commands but did not examine the response. This caused the client and server to agree to use an extension the firewall did not understand, breaking the protocol exchange. A firewall acting as an SMTP endpoint must scan EHLO responses and only allow extensions it understands through.
sections.eli5: When messages say "I need this to get through", the firewall has to understand what that means or let it through. Just saying yes without understanding breaks things.

sections.title: Application Protocol Design Considerations
sections.content:
As firewalls became widespread, applications had to be designed with them in mind. RFC 2979 sets expectations for application designers.

Application protocols SHOULD be designed to facilitate operation across firewalls, as long as this does not harm the application in other ways. Application specifications MAY include material defining requirements firewalls must meet to properly handle the protocol.

Good application design includes defining a secure subset of the protocol, specifying appropriate firewall traversal mechanisms (like SOCKS), and registering separate ports for new protocols rather than wrapping them in port 80 (HTTP) to bypass firewalls. Wrapping protocols in HTTP is a poor idea because it eventually adds complexity to firewall handling of port 80 and breaks the transparency principle.
sections.eli5: New applications should be designed to work with firewalls in mind, but not by disguising themselves as HTTP to sneak through.
